clue.text: Company whose rep made no report on Canterbury trip

definitions.text: Company whose rep made no report on Canterbury trip

blocks.clueFragment: Company whose rep made no report
blocks.note: surface reading: a firm whose sales representative failed to file a report
setter's reading: a London livery company whose representative among Chaucer's Canterbury pilgrims tells no tale

explanation.surface: A firm's travelling salesman comes back from a trip to Canterbury without writing anything up.
explanation.walkthrough: In Chaucer's Canterbury Tales the Haberdasher rides with the pilgrims but is never given a tale. The Haberdashers are also one of the City of London's livery companies, hence 'Company'.
explanation.definitionFit: The livery guild of dealers in sewing goods is a London company, and Chaucer's pilgrim from that trade tells no story.

clue.text: It's difficult to hold a horse, say, if untamed

indicators.note: a word that holds something keeps it inside, so the other pieces sit within it

blocks.note: hard means difficult
taken as written
gee-gee is nursery talk for a horse, written GG; 'say' marks it as an example

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that it is hard to keep hold of a horse that has never been broken in.
explanation.walkthrough: HARD holds A and GG. 'It's' just sets up the sentence. In falconry a haggard is a hawk caught wild as an adult, so the word first meant untamed.
explanation.definitionFit: Falconers called a wild-caught adult hawk haggard, meaning wild and intractable, which is an older sense than gaunt.

clue.text: New York's way to put on shows

definitions.text: New York's way to put on shows

blocks.clueFragment: New York's way to put on shows
blocks.note: surface reading: the manner in which New York stages its theatre
setter's reading: the famous New York theatre street, with its second half 'way' already given in the clue

explanation.surface: How New York goes about staging its shows.
explanation.walkthrough: Broadway is the New York street of theatres. The clue supplies 'way', so the answer is the part that goes in front of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Add 'way' to the five letters and you get the Manhattan street whose theatres put on the city's big shows.

clue.text: City Jane loved

blocks.note: first meaning: a cathedral city in Kent, also a city in New York State
second meaning: the man Jane Eyre loves in Charlotte Brontë's novel

explanation.walkthrough: Jane is Jane Eyre, whose employer and eventual husband is Edward Fairfax Rochester.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is both a Kentish cathedral city and Charlotte Brontë's brooding hero whom her governess heroine marries.

clue.text: Lincoln died thus (the day after shooting)

definitions.text: Lincoln died thus (the day after shooting)

blocks.note: surface reading: asks how the president met his death, inviting an answer about the assassination
setter's reading: shot at the theatre, he survived the night and died next morning lying in his bed

explanation.surface: A history question about the manner of Abraham Lincoln's death after he was shot.
explanation.walkthrough: Lincoln was shot at Ford's Theatre in the evening and died the next morning in a lodging house across the street; the answer is where, not how violently.
explanation.definitionFit: Lincoln did not die on the spot but lying in bed the following morning, which is what the old adverb meaning in bed describes.

clue.text: Governor gets prize as patriotic leader

indicators.note: one part acquires the other, so they are joined one after the other

blocks.note: HE, His Excellency, is the title of a colonial governor
a prize is a reward

explanation.surface: A colonial governor is honoured as a patriot who led his people.
explanation.walkthrough: Hereward the Wake led English resistance to the Norman conquerors in the Fens around 1070.
explanation.definitionFit: The Anglo-Saxon rebel is remembered as a native hero who led a fight against the invading Normans.

clue.text: Thus put off return of outcast

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the word is read from its end

blocks.note: a leper is a social outcast

explanation.surface: Someone sent away and now coming back is shunned once again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thus' points from the wordplay to the meaning: the turnaround of an outcast is a word for put off.
explanation.definitionFit: To repel someone is to drive them away or disgust them, which is what put off means as a verb.

clue.text: Play a part in breaking learner in

indicators.note: a part of something lies inside it, so the answer is a run of letters within the next words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of breaking and the start of learner

explanation.surface: Taking a small role while training up a novice.
explanation.walkthrough: The final 'in' only completes the phrase 'breaking in', the training of a beginner; the Shakespeare tragedy is hidden in brea-KING LEAR-ner.
explanation.definitionFit: The tragedy about an old monarch dividing his realm among his daughters is one of Shakespeare's plays.

clue.text: Announces conditions

blocks.note: first meaning: declares, a verb
second meaning: situations or circumstances, a plural noun

explanation.surface: Someone sets out the terms of a deal.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb for declaring formally and also the plural noun for situations, as in states of affairs.

clue.text: First-class fare brought in annually at Christmas

blocks.note: first meaning: excellent food and drink, fare in its sense of food
second meaning: what the old rhyme says Christmas brings when it comes once a year

explanation.surface: A top-quality ticket bought each year for Christmas travel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fare' looks like a ticket price but means food. The rhyme runs 'Christmas comes but once a year, and when it comes it brings good cheer'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheer once meant food and drink, so fine cheer is fine fare, and the festive phrase is what Christmas proverbially brings.

clue.text: This is for publication - that's positive

blocks.note: first meaning: a verb used when copy is passed to be published, as in 'all the news that's fit to'
second meaning: in photography, the image made from a negative

explanation.surface: A firm statement that something is going on the record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Positive' reads as 'certain', but it is the photographic positive made from a negative.
explanation.definitionFit: To put something into type is to make it public, and a photographic copy developed from a negative is also called by this word.

clue.text: Peter's brother once more brings in the doctor

indicators.note: to bring someone in is to take them inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: anew means again, once more
DR is the abbreviation for doctor

explanation.surface: A man's sibling calls the doctor in again.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter is the apostle Simon Peter, whose brother was also one of the twelve.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Gospels the fisherman apostle was the brother of Simon Peter and brought him to Jesus.

clue.text: Chance upon wit, roamin' in the gloamin'

indicators.note: something roaming wanders about, so the letters stray from their order

blocks.note: the three letters of wit, rearranged
to light on or upon something is to chance upon it

explanation.surface: Quoting the old song 'Roamin' in the Gloamin'', a stroller happens to find wit on an evening walk.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of wit comes first, then LIGHT. 'Roamin' in the Gloamin'' is a Harry Lauder music-hall song; gloaming is a Scots word for dusk.
explanation.definitionFit: Gloaming is a Scots and poetic word for evening dusk, the half-dark after sunset.

clue.text: Substitute North African chief put in

indicators.note: the word put in tells the solver that one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a dey was the ruler of Algiers or Tunis under the Ottomans
taken as written

explanation.surface: A North African ruler is replaced by a stand-in.
explanation.walkthrough: The dey, the Ottoman-era governor of Algiers, is an old crossword favourite; here he is the container, with 'in' telling you the other piece goes inside him.
explanation.definitionFit: A deputy acts in place of someone else, so as a noun the word means a stand-in or replacement.

clue.text: Little girl, we hear, put on dress for Eliot's man

indicators.note: what we hear is a spoken name, so the letters follow its sound rather than its spelling
in a down clue one part placed on another sits above it, so they join in order

blocks.note: Prue is a short girl's name, here written to match its sound
a frock is a dress

explanation.surface: A small girl puts on a dress to play a character from Eliot.
explanation.walkthrough: J. Alfred Prufrock is the speaker of T. S. Eliot's poem 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock'.
explanation.definitionFit: The timid narrator of T. S. Eliot's 1915 love-song poem is named J. Alfred Prufrock.

clue.text: Crazy cryptanalysts?

blocks.note: first meaning: mad, informal adjective
second meaning: people who crack codes, read whimsically as a noun

explanation.surface: Are code-breakers out of their minds?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the whimsical second sense: those who crack ciphers.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is British slang for mad, and taken literally it names people who break codes.

clue.text: Oscar's way of manipulating characters gets the bird

indicators.note: handling the letters freely moves them into a fresh order

blocks.note: the letters of the two words, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Oscar has a habit of manipulating people, and gets booed for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets the bird' is slang for being jeered, which makes 'bird' look like an idiom; the cassowary is a large flightless bird of Australia and New Guinea.
explanation.definitionFit: The cassowary is a big flightless bird related to the emu, found in New Guinea and northern Australia.

clue.text: Dodging about at home and abroad

blocks.note: someone at home is in
taken as written
abroad here means out and about, away from home

explanation.surface: Someone darts about, both in their own country and overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abroad' looks like overseas, but it is used in its older sense of outdoors.
explanation.definitionFit: Weaving in and out is moving back and forth, which is what dodging about does.

clue.text: Pointedly encouraging - second 23's pleased response

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
23 is the tomcat, and a contented cat purrs

explanation.surface: Someone eggs another on, getting a happy reply from the tomcat of the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pointedly' is literal: spurs are pointed, so spurring urges a horse on with something sharp.
explanation.definitionFit: Spurs are pointed, so urging someone on with them is literally encouraging with points.

clue.text: Composer had right to a meal

indicators.note: one part has taken the other on, so it follows straight after

blocks.note: Franz von Suppé wrote the Light Cavalry and Poet and Peasant overtures
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A composer was entitled to be given a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'had' reads as part of 'had right to', but it means the composer took on the abbreviation; Suppé is an Austrian composer of light operetta.
explanation.definitionFit: Supper is the evening meal, so the word is a noun naming one particular meal.

clue.text: Legendary Egyptian king's huge flag

blocks.note: OS stands for outsize, the clothing size
flag is another name for the iris plant

explanation.surface: A mythical pharaoh flies an enormous banner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flag' looks like a banner, but the yellow flag is a wild iris.
explanation.definitionFit: In Egyptian myth he was the king murdered by his brother Set who became ruler of the dead.

clue.text: Edith's family have good seats

definitions.note: a verb phrase, read as two words

blocks.note: first meaning: the surname of the poet Edith and her literary brothers
second meaning: to ride or sit gracefully, as on a horse, read as two words

explanation.surface: A family named after its matriarch gets the best places at a show.
explanation.walkthrough: Edith Sitwell, poet, and her brothers Osbert and Sacheverell were a famous English literary family. To sit well is to have a good seat, as on a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet Dame Edith belonged to the eccentric literary trio of siblings bearing that surname.

clue.text: Trooper gave information about a league in Persia

blocks.note: a para is a paratrooper
to sing is slang for informing to the police

explanation.surface: A soldier informs on someone, perhaps about a sports league in Iran.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' means approximately, since the Persian unit is roughly a league long.
explanation.definitionFit: The parasang was an old Persian measure of distance of about three and a half miles, close to a league.

clue.text: Share out the port

blocks.note: first meaning: divide among people, a verb
second meaning: a harbour city on the Dalmatian coast of Croatia

explanation.surface: Pour round the port after dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The port' reads as the after-dinner drink, but it is the Adriatic seaport.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means divide up among several people and is also the name of a Croatian harbour city.

clue.text: He aims to mate with queen

definitions.text: He aims to mate with queen

blocks.clueFragment: He aims to mate with queen
blocks.note: surface reading: a chess player planning to checkmate using the queen
setter's reading: a queen is a female cat, and he is the male who wants to breed with her

explanation.surface: A chess player plans to deliver checkmate with his queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Breeders call a female cat a queen, which turns the chess picture into a cat's love life.
explanation.definitionFit: A male cat seeks out a female, which breeders call a queen, to mate.

clue.text: Go up from about, £1 to a thousand on opening of bidding

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its start, so only its first letter is used

blocks.note: C is circa, about
L for pound and I for one
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
the first letter of bidding

explanation.surface: At auction the bidding rises from a pound to a thousand once it opens.
explanation.walkthrough: '£1' gives two pieces, L for the pound sign and I for one.
explanation.definitionFit: To climb is to ascend, which is exactly what go up means as a verb.

clue.text: Pie for communal meal

blocks.note: first meaning: printer's pie, type jumbled into confusion
second meaning: a meal eaten together, as in the officers' dining hall

explanation.surface: A pie served up at a shared dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: Pie is a printers' word for spilled, jumbled type, hence a muddle.
explanation.definitionFit: Printers called jumbled type pie, a muddle; and in the services the word names a shared meal or dining place.

clue.text: Top general making a comeback about 90

indicators.note: coming back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the name runs from its end
something placed about another surrounds it

blocks.note: Robert E. Lee, the Confederate general
XC is 90 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A senior general returns to service at the age of ninety.
explanation.walkthrough: The general is Robert E. Lee of the American Confederacy, a crossword staple; 'Top' is a verb here, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: To top is to outdo or surpass, which is exactly what excelling means as a verb.

clue.text: Effective worker

blocks.note: first meaning: in force, functioning, an adjective
second meaning: a factory hand or machine operator, a noun

explanation.surface: An employee who gets things done.
explanation.definitionFit: A rule in force is said to be operative, and a person who operates machinery in a factory is also called this.

clue.text: A sign of rank snobbery?

blocks.note: surface reading: rank as an adjective, snobbery that is offensively gross
setter's reading: rank as a noun, a possession that signals social standing to snobs

explanation.surface: Some sign shows that a person is a thoroughly rank snob.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rank' wants to be an adjective meaning outright; read it as a noun, social position.
explanation.definitionFit: A showy possession that advertises one's social standing is exactly what a snob displays.
